title: Buying Time

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Is aging a process we simply have to accept as a fact of life? A philosopher would say yes. Many doctors would agree: our cells eventually reach the point where they can no longer divide, and either die or reach retirement phase. Most scientists believe in the idea of limited somatic cell division which says no one can live past about 120 years. But an increasing number of people including gerontologists, biologists, and engineers, believe that aging is a disease, and one that can be cured. They believe aging is not an immutable process but one we can change through scientific advances, drugs and lifestyle changes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Since 1900, the average life expectancy has risen from 47.3 years to 78 years in the U.S., which is about a 60% increase. It is quite possible that scientists will be able to prolong healthy living as opposed to just 'life'. Gerontologists and others in the field are not concerned with prolonging end-of-life stages, when we are at our weakest, unhealthiest point. Today's search is for longer and healthier life. It is about turning back our biological clocks to be younger for longer. They believe in the 'longevity dividend'; that is the economic benefits of extending healthy lives, including reduced spending on healthcare, and an increase in contributions to society.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the most promising avenues of anti-aging research comes from inside our own bodies: the telomere. Derived from the Greek nouns telos (end) and meros (part), these 'end parts' are at the tips of our chromosomes, serving as protective caps for preserving genetic information. Without them, genomes would lose information after cell division. A cell's age can be measured by the length of its telomeres. Telomeres also prevent a cell's chromosomes from fusing with each other. When cells divide, telomeres shorten. When telomeres reach their shortest point, cells stop dividing or die. These senescent cells sometimes called age-related diseases, increase wrinkles on the skin and weaken our immune and other systems.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In 2009, the Nobel prize in physiology or medicine was awarded to Elizabeth Blackburn and her team for their 1984 discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme, telomerase. Telomerase is a protein that stabilises telomeres when they get worn, or causes them to lengthen and aids cell division. Three months later, a genetics team at the Longevity Project, at the Institute for Aging Research at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, discovered a correlation between people living to 100 and inheriting a mutant gene that makes their telomerase-maintaining system extra active and able to maintain telomere length more effectively. For the most part, these people were spared age-related diseases such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes. In March 2009, researchers at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark mapped telomerase for the first time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: According to Dr Michael Fossell, one of the authors of The Immortality Edge, the key to immortality is turning the telomerase gene from off to on. He believes that soon there will be a drug therapy that will turn on the telomerase gene in healthy cells thereby extending the telomere and reversing aging. However, aside from TA-65, a controversial and expensive supplement, there have not yet been any solutions to finding this ‘on’ switch to produce the protein that would lengthen our telomeres. Besides, genetic factors account for only 30% of what happens to us, according to the Human Genome Project. This means that 70% is environmental, so there’s a lot that can be done by the individual to protect cells.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Stress, for example, is bad for us. Stressed people look older and evidence shows this on a cellular level as well. In a 2009 article in the journal Hormones, Dr Elissa Appel of the University of California, San Francisco found that stress, coupled with overeating, 'appears to be conducive to several cell-aging mechanisms, mainly dampening telomerase and leading to telomere length reduction'. She also found that chronic stress may weaken our immune system, causing us to age faster. In later studies that Appel did, mothers of children with chronic illness were compared with mothers of healthy children. The mothers of children with chronic illness had shorter telomeres and less telomerase. There was no genetic component, proving that our telomeres are indeed affected by stress. In 2009 Dr Christian Werner, of the University of Hamburg in Germany, compared men living sedentary lives with those who ran more than 72 kilometres a week. There was a significant difference in the telomere length of older men in their 50s: the sedentary older men had telomeres 40% shorter than fitter, older men. Then, in a 2010 study, Tonya Jacobs compared a group of people who had meditated for three months with another similar group who had not, and found that telomerase activity was significantly greater in those who meditated. As far as diet is concerned, results are very mixed, but a 2010 study published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found that fibre, waist size and saturated fats all affected telomere length in older women. In short, a recognised healthy diet such as the Mediterranean diet, together with a reduction in sugar, has been shown to protect our cells.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: However, the secret to immortality is not the real issue at stake. Understanding telomeres is only the first step to eliminating processes of aging and oxidative stress, that is the damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids (fats) caused by oxidants. It is to be anticipated that science will continue to develop answers on how to cure diseases associated with aging, and therefore help us to lengthen our healthy lives.
